text:
B: Hello, can you hear me? I am Bożena.
A: Yes. Hi. Jurgita.
B: Jurgita. This is Lithuanian name, I think?
A: Yes. From Šiauliai. You are Polish?
B: Yes, from Olsztyn. Not so far from you, really, in the north.
A: Yes, not far. I live in Wakefield now. Fifteen years, nearly.
B: I am in Southampton, since 2006. Nearly twenty years. How quickly it goes. What do you do, Jurgita?
A: Senior care assistant. Care home, old people. Twelve-hour shifts.
B: Oh, that is hard work. You do the medicines also?
A: Yes. MAR charts, medication round, morning and evening.
B: MAR charts! I know these very well. I was pharmacy technician eleven years. We did the blister packs for some care homes in Shirley. Always, always a phone call, the chart does not match.
A: Yes! Always. Doctor changes something, pharmacy does not know, and we are in the middle. Last month we waited three days for one lady's tablets. Three days. And manager says to me, why you did not chase? I chased. Every day I phoned.
B: I believe you. Sometimes it was us, sometimes the surgery, sometimes nobody knows. I am sorry, I think I was on the other end of these phone calls.
A: Is okay. You are not my pharmacy.
B: No, and not anymore, the branch closed. So now I am looking for part-time. Maybe a hospital.
A: Hospital is better. More money, more steady.
B: I hope so. You have family here?
A: Husband, Darius. He is Lithuanian also. He drives forklift. My mum and sister are in Lithuania still.
B: My mother also, she is eighty-four, in Olsztyn. My sister looks after her. I go once or twice a year. Is not enough, I think.
A: Yes. My mum is alone. My sister is in same town, but she is teacher, she works a lot. Every Sunday my mum phones and asks, did you go to Mass, did you eat. I say yes.
B: Ha, every mother is the same. Do you go to Mass here?
A: In Leeds, Polish and Lithuanian. Christmas and Easter. Sometimes more.
B: I go to the Polish parish most Sundays. And at Easter we do the blessing of the basket, the eggs, the bread, the sausage. You do this also, in Lithuania?
A: Eggs, yes. We paint eggs. My mum does them still, very nice ones, with wax.
B: Oh, beautiful. You cook Lithuanian food here?
A: Simple. Potatoes, soup. Cepelinai only at Christmas, is too much work. I buy sausage and bread from shop on Kirkgate.
B: Same for me, the Polish shop on Portswood Road. But they run out of the good twaróg again, every week, I don't know why.
A: Our shop also. Good things, gone by Saturday.
B: We should complain together, I think.
A: Yes. I am very good at complaining.
B: Ha! I believe this also. You know, Jurgita, when I first came here, I was very lonely, I cried in the evenings sometimes. Was it like this for you?
A: Sometimes. Still, sometimes. Here I am foreign, there I am, you know, English one. Is strange.
B: Yes. I know exactly. Between two places. But I think—
